data.title: Norway wealth fund weighs $80B cut to U.S. Treasury holdings
data.description:
Norway’s $2.3 trillion sovereign wealth fund has recommended reducing its government-bond holdings and shifting money into higher-yielding fixed-income assets.

Norges Bank Investment Management proposed lowering government debt from 70% to 50% of the fund’s bond benchmark. The change could remove about $106 billion from global sovereign bonds, including nearly $80 billion from U.S. Treasuries, the Financial Times estimated.

The fund would redirect much of that money into assets such as agency mortgage-backed securities. These bonds carry credit quality similar to Treasuries because they are supported by Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac or Ginnie Mae, but typically offer higher yields to compensate investors for the risk that homeowners repay mortgages early.

For investors, the proposal is another sign that major institutional buyers are demanding better returns from their bond portfolios as government borrowing rises and yields remain elevated. An $80 billion reduction would be small relative to the enormous Treasury market, but similar moves by other reserve managers could weaken demand for U.S. debt and add upward pressure to yields. The shift also suggests that highly rated mortgage securities may become more attractive alternatives to government bonds.

The changes would leave the fund’s overall U.S. dollar exposure largely intact. Its Treasury weighting would fall by 12.2 percentage points, while its allocation to other U.S. fixed-income securities would rise by 11.4 points. Holdings of British government bonds would remain steady, while Japanese sovereign debt would gain a larger weighting.

NBIM also recommended weighting government bonds according to the value of each country’s outstanding debt rather than the size of its economy. The fund said the broader overhaul would diversify its sources of fixed-income returns while preserving sufficient liquidity during periods of market stress.

The recommendation isn't final. An expert council is expected to submit broader advice to Norway’s finance ministry by January, with the government scheduled to present its proposal to parliament in spring 2027, according to the Financial Times.

data.title: Iran claims strike on U.S. drone vessel as Hormuz fighting escalates
data.description:
Iran said Sunday that its forces struck an unmanned U.S. vessel attempting to enter the Strait of Hormuz, extending a renewed exchange of attacks between the two countries. The U.S. military had not confirmed Iran’s claim, the Associated Press reported.

The reported strike followed U.S. attacks on three Iranian oil tankers Saturday. Washington said those operations were retaliation for Iranian missile fire directed at U.S. Navy warships.

The latest clashes ended about a month of relative calm. Fighting began with U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran on Feb. 28 and has continued intermittently despite a ceasefire announced in June. Diplomatic efforts subsequently broke down, leaving Iran’s nuclear program and control of shipping through the strait unresolved. 

For investors, the escalation raises the risk of further disruption to one of the world’s most important oil and liquefied-natural-gas corridors. Threats to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz could lift crude prices, tanker rates and insurance costs while weighing on airlines, transportation companies and other fuel-intensive businesses. Continued fighting could also increase demand for defense contractors and traditional safe-haven assets.

The Trump administration has combined military action with financial pressure on institutions that handle Iranian funds. Tehran, meanwhile, has continued exporting some oil through a network of vessels designed to evade sanctions and the U.S. blockade.

Iran’s influence over traffic through the strait has become one of its principal sources of leverage as the U.S. and European allies consider referring Tehran to the U.N. Security Council over alleged violations of its nuclear obligations.

data.title: Three ways the midterms could move markets - BofA
data.description:
The U.S. midterm elections are unlikely to amount to a true “regime change” for markets, but BofA strategist Michael Hartnett says the outcome could still produce sharply different reactions across stocks, bonds and the dollar.

Hartnett argues the midterms are unlikely to alter the broader fiscal trajectory in Washington. In his view, the 2020s remain a decade of political populism, with both the right and left favoring spending to maintain support. That backdrop has helped drive what he calls a period of fiscal excess, strong nominal GDP growth and an “Anything But Bonds” strategic allocation environment.

Investors have also appeared relatively relaxed about the election, Hartnett said, in part because President Donald Trump has governed heavily through executive orders and because the Senate map remains difficult for Democrats.

In BofA’s August Fund Manager Survey, 47% of respondents said the most likely result was a Republican Senate and Democratic House. Another 23% expected a Democratic sweep, while 9% saw Republicans retaining control of both chambers.

But Hartnett noted that the odds of a Democratic sweep have been rising. Trump’s approval rating, at roughly 35%-40%, is well below the historical average for presidents two months ahead of midterm elections, while Polymarket recently put the probability of a Democratic sweep at 50%, versus 35% for a Republican Senate and Democratic House and 10% for a GOP sweep.

BofA sees three main market scenarios:

  • A Democratic sweep would be the biggest risk-off outcome. Hartnett said it could trigger a more than 10% decline in stocks (SPY) (IVV) (VOO) (QQQ) (DIA) (IWM) (MDY) into year-end, alongside a weaker U.S. dollar (DXY) and lower bond yields (SHY) (IEI) (IEF) (TBT) (TLT). International equities (URTH) would likely outperform, with Europe favored over Asia. BofA’s preferred hedge for that outcome is short Financials (XLF) and the dollar.
  • A Republican sweep would be the strongest risk-on scenario, giving a “green light” to the AI trade and supporting the dollar as the U.S. exceptionalism theme returns.
  • The most likely middle ground, a Republican Senate and Democratic House, would be modestly risk-on. Hartnett’s shorthand: “gridlock = goldilocks.”

data.title: Earnings Week Ahead: ORCL, ADBE, KR, GME, CHWY, and more
data.description:
Despite a relatively light earnings calendar, the upcoming week features a range of notable reports across technology, retail, and consumer goods, led by a heavyweight technology lineup, with Oracle (ORCL) and Adobe (ADBE) headlining Thursday's results and offering fresh reads on enterprise AI spending, cloud demand, and software budgets. Copart (CPRT) will also report Thursday, while Kroger (KR) closes out the week with an update on grocery demand and consumer trends.

The broader slate spans retail, consumer, aerospace, healthcare, and emerging technology. Macy's (M), Chewy (CHWY), American Eagle Outfitters (AEO), and Casey's General Stores (CASY) will provide insight into discretionary spending and consumer resilience, while AeroVironment (AVAV) offers a read on defense demand. United Natural Foods (UNFI) will add another perspective on grocery and food distribution trends.

The more speculative end of the calendar includes Nano-X Imaging (NNOX), Agenus (AGEN), and Canaan (CAN), bringing medical technology, biotechnology, and crypto-mining exposure into an otherwise consumer and technology-focused week.

Below is a rundown of major quarterly updates anticipated in the week of September 7 to September 11:

Monday, September 7

US markets will remain closed in observance of the Labor Day holiday.

Tuesday, September 8

GameStop (GME)

GameStop (GME) is set to report its Q2 results after Tuesday’s close, following preliminary figures released last week that showed net income nearly doubling Y/Y despite a sharp decline in sales. The results highlight a widening gap between the company’s underlying operating performance and gains from its investment portfolio, leaving investors focused on the outlook for the core business and capital allocation.

On August 31, GameStop projected Q2 net sales of $780M to $800M, down from $972.2M a year earlier, reflecting the difficult comparison from the prior-year Nintendo Switch 2 launch, planned store closures, and the divestiture of its France operations. Operating income, however, is expected at $150M to $170M, up from $66.4M, while net income is projected at $290M to $310M versus $168.6M a year earlier. About $238M of the projected net income is expected to come from mark-to-market gains on GameStop’s 43.4M eBay shares, valued at roughly $4.95B. With the headline figures already disclosed, the focus will shift to forward commentary, the company’s eBay strategy, and the implications of its recently amended debt exchange.

On capital allocation, GameStop amended its previously announced exchange of approximately $1.4B of convertible notes, with noteholders now set to receive about 55.5M shares and $358.4M in cash. Following the exchange, approximately $2.8B of convertible notes will remain outstanding. Separately, reports in August indicated that CEO Ryan Cohen was considering withdrawing GameStop’s $56B bid for eBay in favor of a potential partnership or joint venture, although no final decision had been announced.

Options markets are pricing in a 9.04% move in either direction around Tuesday's full results.

  • Consensus EPS Estimate: $0.27
  • Consensus Revenue Estimate: $756.85M
  • Earnings Insight: GameStop has beaten EPS estimates in 7 of the past 8 quarters, exceeding revenue expectations just once in that span.

Also reporting: Canaan (CAN), United Natural Foods (UNFI), Casey's General Stores (CASY), ABM Industries (ABM), MIND Technology (MIND), and more.

Wednesday, September 9

Chewy (CHWY)

Chewy (CHWY), the online pet products and services retailer, is set to report its Q2 results before the market opens on Wednesday, with investors looking for signs that recurring Autoship growth and newer businesses can offset pressure from a softer consumer environment.

In Q1, Chewy reported revenue of $3.12B, up 6.3% Y/Y, while adjusted EPS of $0.35 beat the $0.34 consensus estimate. Autoship accounted for approximately 84% of net sales, continuing to provide a substantial recurring revenue base. Management guided full-year sales to $13.40B-$13.55B, citing macroeconomic pressure and consumer trade-down to lower-priced pet products, with the outlook contributing to a sharp post-earnings selloff.

On recent developments, Mizuho lowered its price target to $32 from $40 while maintaining an Outperform rating, while Raymond James raised its target to $28 from $25 and Bank of America reiterated a Buy rating. Investors will also be watching Chewy's expansion in veterinary care following its acquisition of Modern Animal, with the company targeting approximately 60 Chewy Vet Care locations by the end of 2026. AI-driven cost savings and growth in sponsored advertising will be additional areas of focus as Chewy looks to expand its higher-margin revenue streams.

Wall Street rates the stock a Buy, while Seeking Alpha's Quant Rating holds a more cautious Hold.

  • Consensus EPS Estimate: $0.36
  • Consensus Revenue Estimate: $3.32B
  • Earnings Insight: Chewy has beaten revenue estimates in 8 straight quarters and EPS estimates in 5 of those reports.

Also reporting: Nano-X Imaging (NNOX), American Eagle Outfitters (AEO), AeroVironment (AVAV), Signet Jewelers (SIG), SailPoint (SAIL), Academy Sports and Outdoors (ASO), Lakeland Industries (LAKE), and more.

Thursday, September 10

Adobe (ADBE)

Adobe (ADBE), the creative and digital experience software provider, is set to report its fiscal Q3 2026 results after Thursday’s close, with investors weighing continued AI-driven growth against an ongoing leadership transition and elevated expectations for recurring revenue.

In Q2 FY2026, Adobe reported record revenue of $6.62B, up 13% Y/Y, while non-GAAP EPS of $5.96 marked its fifth consecutive quarterly beat. AI-first ARR tripled Y/Y to more than $500M, while total ARR reached $27.10B at the end of the quarter. Management raised its full-year FY2026 revenue guidance to $26.50B-$26.60B and non-GAAP EPS guidance to $24.35-$24.45. For Q3, Adobe guided revenue to $6.67B-$6.72B and non-GAAP EPS to $6.05-$6.10, putting the focus on ARR growth, AI monetization, and the company’s ability to sustain its recent execution.

The leadership picture has also become clearer ahead of the print. Adobe announced on September 3 that Anil Chakravarthy will become president and CEO on December 1, with Shantanu Narayen transitioning to executive chair. Steve Day is serving as interim CFO following Dan Durn’s departure. Meanwhile, Adobe agreed in June to acquire AI video and image enhancement company Topaz Labs, with the transaction expected to close in the second half of 2026. Investors will be watching ARR growth, AI-first ARR, Creative and Document Cloud trends, FY2026 guidance, and management’s initial commentary on the leadership transition and FY2027 outlook.

Options markets are pricing in a 5.4% move in either direction for Thursday's print.

Wall Street's and Seeking Alpha’s Quant Rating both rate the stock a Hold.

  • Consensus EPS Estimate: $6.09
  • Consensus Revenue Estimate: $6.70B
  • Earnings Insight: Adobe has exceeded EPS and revenue estimates in each of the past eight quarters.

Oracle Corporation (ORCL)

Oracle (ORCL) is set to report its FQ1 results after Thursday’s close, with investors seeking evidence that the company can convert its extraordinary AI-driven backlog into accelerating revenue while managing the heavy capital requirements behind its cloud infrastructure expansion.

In Q4 FY2026, Oracle reported record revenue of $19.2B, up 21% Y/Y, while cloud infrastructure revenue surged 93% to $5.8B. Full-year FY2026 revenue reached $67.4B, up 17%, with total cloud revenue rising 39% to $34.0B. Remaining performance obligations jumped 363% Y/Y to $638B, fueled largely by large AI infrastructure contracts. For Q1 FY2027, Oracle guided revenue growth of 27%-29% and cloud revenue growth of 58%-64%, while setting non-GAAP EPS guidance at $1.72-$1.76. Management also maintained its $90B FY2027 revenue target and raised non-GAAP EPS guidance to $8.05.

The scale of Oracle's AI opportunity remains the central catalyst, but so do questions around execution and capital intensity. Citi placed Oracle on a positive catalyst watch in August following the stock's steep pullback, maintaining a Buy rating and a $330 price target. Meanwhile, bearish analysts have pointed to data-center capacity constraints, funding requirements, and customer concentration as risks to converting the massive RPO balance into revenue. Oracle expects to raise approximately $40B through debt and equity financing in FY2027 after raising $48B in FY2026, while free cash flow was negative $23.7B last year as the company accelerated AI infrastructure investment.

Investors will be watching cloud infrastructure growth, RPO conversion, capital expenditures, and free cash flow, as well as any updates to the $90B FY2027 revenue target and $8.05 non-GAAP EPS outlook. The pace at which Oracle converts its AI backlog into reported revenue will be particularly important given the increasingly capital-intensive nature of its expansion.

Wall Street rates ORCL a Buy, while Seeking Alpha's Quant Rating holds a more cautious Hold.

  • Consensus EPS Estimate: $1.74
  • Consensus Revenue Estimate: $19.13B
  • Earnings Insight: Oracle has exceeded EPS estimates in 5 of the past 8 quarters and revenue estimates in only 4 of those reports.

Also reporting: Macy's (M), RH (RH), Copart (CPRT), Designer Brands (DBI), and more.

Friday, September 11

The Kroger (KR)

Kroger (KR), the nation's largest supermarket operator, is set to report its fiscal Q2 FY2027 results before Friday's open, with investors looking for insight that the company's investments in e-commerce, pricing, and productivity can translate into stronger comparable sales and margin performance in the second half of the year.

In Q1 FY2027, Kroger reported sales of $46.1B, up from $45.1B a year earlier, while identical sales excluding fuel increased 1.0% and adjusted e-commerce sales rose 19%. Adjusted EPS came in at $1.58, up from $1.49 a year earlier, while operating profit increased to $1.41B from $1.32B. Management maintained its full-year outlook for identical sales growth of 1%-2%, adjusted FIFO operating profit of $5.0B-$5.2B, and EPS of $5.10-$5.30. The relatively modest comparable-sales growth leaves the company needing stronger momentum in the back half of the year to reach the upper end of its outlook.

On recent developments, Kroger named Nate Faust as executive vice president and chief eCommerce officer, effective September 1, bringing additional digital leadership as the company works to improve the profitability of its online business. Separately, Kroger agreed in July to acquire Giant Eagle for $1.65B, adding 197 supermarkets and 11 standalone pharmacies across several Midwestern and Mid-Atlantic states. The transaction is expected to close in 2027, subject to regulatory clearance. Investors will be watching comparable sales, e-commerce profitability, gross-margin trends, and any updates to full-year guidance, as well as management's commentary on the Giant Eagle deal and the consumer spending environment.

Wall Street rates KR a Buy, while Seeking Alpha's Quant Rating holds a more cautious Hold.

  • Consensus EPS Estimate: $1.05
  • Consensus Revenue Estimate: $34.78B
  • Earnings Insight: Kroger has beaten EPS estimates in 7 of the past 8 quarters and revenue once in that time frame.

Also reporting: Cheetah Mobile (CMCM), Hooker Furnishings (HOFT), and more.

data.title: Paris climate goal likely out of reach, United Nations report says
data.description:
The Paris climate agreement goal of limiting the rise in global temperatures to 1.5 degrees Celsius is no longer feasible and likely will be exceeded within the next few years, according to a report released this week by the United Nations.

"While the international community has made progress on climate change, global action to cut greenhouse gas emissions has not been fast enough to avoid global warming crossing 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels in the next few years," which means the long-term temperature goal of the Paris Agreement to keep warming below 1.5 degrees would not be within reach, the U.N. said in the report.

"Across the globe, extreme heatwaves are already proving that climate impacts will strike faster, hit harder, and last longer—costing more lives and causing deeper disruption," U.N. Environment Programme Director Inger Andersen said.

The report described an "overshoot" scenario in which global warming exceeds 1.5 degrees Celsius in the next few years, then peaks before gradually declining, with the goal of bringing temperatures back below the 1.5 mark by the end of the century.

The U.N. said the "most optimistic scenario," if governments fully implement their climate plans and meet net-zero targets, would see peak temperatures reach 1.8 degrees Celsius.

Under current policies, however, the report predicted global warming could reach 2.6 degrees Celsius by 2100, with a range of 1.9-3.6 degrees Celsius by 2100, and noted that policymakers now should "prepare for and navigate a future in which global temperatures exceed 1.5 degrees Celsius."

data.title: Key deals this week: Flex, Nvidia, AbbVie and more
data.description:
Here's a list of key deals reported across sectors this week:

Flex (FLEX) on Thursday said it will acquire digital power infrastructure provider EPC Power at a value of $4.4 billion, aiming to add power conversion capabilities for AI data centers and grid applications. The deal is expected to close in the fourth quarter of calendar 2026, at which time California-based EPC Power is expected to become part of Flex's Cloud and Power Infrastructure, or CPI, segment, Flex said.

Nvidia (NVDA) confirmed prior media reports on Thursday when it announced it had agreed to purchase Hugging Face for $12.9B. Hugging Face will remain an open platform for the entire AI ecosystem, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said in a statement. Nvidia (NVDA) compute will not be required to build on or deploy through Hugging Face.

AbbVie (ABBV) has completed its $10.9 billion acquisition of Apogee Therapeutics (APGE), the company said on Thursday. The deal, which is the pharma giant's largest bolt-on acquisition since 2019, was first reported by The Financial Times in June.

Diversified Energy (DEC) said Wednesday it agreed to acquire ‌privately-held Birch Permian Holdings from Elliott Investment Management for ~$1.8B, in a deal Diversified said will establish it as a premier operator of assets in the Permian Basin.

Adobe (ADBE) has purchased India-based marketing intelligence startup Rilo in a deal involving licensing and team acquisition. Adobe (ADBE) confirmed the agreement to TechCrunch, though it didn't provide any more details. Founded by Georgi Boby and Dhruv Jaglan in 2025, Rilo raised $1 million from investors including PeakXV, DeVC, and Day Zero Ventures at a $10 million valuation, according to the report.

KKR & Co. (KKR) has reached an agreement to acquire A1 Garage Door ​Service, a residential garage door repair and replacement company, for ~$2B, sources familiar ​with the matter told Reuters. The Phoenix, Arizona-headquartered family-owned company employs over 1,000 people across 70+ markets.

Vertiv Holdings (VRT) on Wednesday said its subsidiary, Vertiv Corporation, agreed to acquire UtilityInnovation Group for approximately $1.45B in cash at closing, plus up to $1.15B in earnouts based on EBITDA targets over the next 12 to 24 months.

KKR's (KKR) agreement to sell USI to Aon (AON) for $17B in cash will generate a handsome payoff for the alternative asset manager, whose initial investment in the company in 2017 valued USI at ~$4.3B.

Eli Lilly (LLY) has agreed to acquire Merida Biosciences for up to $2.875B in cash, including an upfront payment and contingent milestone payments. The deal is expected to close in Q4 2026, subject to customary conditions and regulatory approvals.

Genel Energy (GEGYF) plunged 14.6% in London trading Friday after Norwegian oil and gas operator DNO (DTNOF) (DTNOY) said it will not make an offer to acquire its British peer. In August, DNO (FTNOF) (FTNOY) made a 69 pence/share takeover approach that valued Genel (GEGYF) at £202M, which the U.K. company dismissed on the grounds that it "fundamentally undervalues" the business; since then, DNO said Genel has "demonstrated no willingness to engage."

data.title: Utilities Sector Underperforms In August; Constellation Energy Gains, PG&E Declines
data.description:
The utilities sector (XLU) underperformed during the month, declining 4.78%, compared with a 2.62% gain for the S&P 500.

Seeking Alpha analyst Louis Gerard said the sector’s August underperformance was driven primarily by a backup in long-term Treasury yields amid rising fiscal deficits and Treasury supply, with growing AI-linked corporate debt also competing with Treasuries.

The higher yields, along with signals that the Fed may need to tighten rather than ease in the coming months, pressured utilities, which typically trade as bond proxies given their stable cash flows, high payouts, and generally low volatility. The sector’s decline pushed utilities into negative territory for the year, making it the only S&P 500 sector down YTD.

Utilities Sector Scorecard

• Sector Return: -4.78%

• Best Performer: Constellation Energy (CEG) (+5.05%)

• Worst Performer: PG&E (PCG) (-26.08%)

Top utility sector performers of August

On the individual front, Constellation Energy (CEG) was the only sector gainer, rising 5.05% during the month. Gerard noted that the stock benefited from a strong quarterly beat-and-raise, with 920 MW of nuclear PPAs signed with investment-grade companies at an average duration of 18.5 years, including a 176 MW agreement with Walmart.

American Water Works (AWK) followed with a 1.77% gain, with Gerard noting there were no specific company-level drivers and that the stock held up as a defensive play amid sector-wide rate volatility.

AES Corporation (AES) also gained 0.72% during the month. Gerard pointed out that the stock now trades largely on merger-arbitrage fundamentals, with the planned acquisition still awaiting further regulatory approvals.

Gerard also noted that these were the only three S&P 500 Utilities constituents to post positive returns during August.

Here are the only three gainers of August:

• Constellation Energy (CEG): +5.05%, Quant rating: Hold with a score of 3.13 out of 5

• American Water Works (AWK): +1.77%, Quant rating: Hold with a score of 2.94 out of 5

• AES Corporation (AES): +0.72%, Quant rating: Hold with a score of 2.97 out of 5

Top utility sector detractors of August

On the other hand, PG&E (PCG) led the sector’s declines, falling 26.08% during the month. Gerard argued that the weakness was linked to Senate Bill 492, which omitted Newsom’s proposed utility liability protections.

These included a provision to bar insurance companies from bringing subrogation suits against utilities, a $6 billion per-incident liability cap, and a wildfire fund replenishment mechanism.

Edison International (EIX) followed with a 22.37% decline. Gerard cited the omission of the same suggested liability protections in Senate Bill 492 as a key concern.

NiSource (NI) declined 8.11% during the month. Gerard attributed the decline mainly to Q2 results showing a falling bottom line, with pressure from a spring lockout at NIPSCO and about $5.4M in non-recurring consulting and severance costs tied to the Value Captured initiative.

Here are the top five detractors of August:

• PG&E (PCG): -26.08%, Quant rating: Hold with a score of 3.03 out of 5

• Edison International (EIX): -22.37%, Quant rating: Hold with a score of 2.97 out of 5

• NiSource (NI): -8.11%, Quant rating: Hold with a score of 2.78 out of 5

• NRG Energy (NRG): -6.46%, Quant rating: Sell with a score of 1.89 out of 5

• Southern Company (SO): -5.99%, Quant rating: Buy with a score of 3.93 out of 5

data.title: Lululemon founder Chip Wilson and wife are getting divorced: report
data.description:
Chip Wilson, the founder of athletic-apparel maker Lululemon Athletica (LULU), and his wife, Shannon "Summer" Wilson, are getting divorced, Bloomberg News reported on Saturday, citing people familiar with the matter.

The couple has discussed their separation plans with friends, the people said, seeking anonymity because conversations are private. 

A family legal proceeding between the two filed in the Supreme Court of British Columbia in April was not accessible by the media or the public. The couple left the yoga clothing company a decade ago but continues to hold a sizable stake in the company.

In 2002, Chip Wilson, 71, one of Canada's wealthiest entrepreneurs, married Summer Wilson, 52, his business partner for more than two decades. According to her website, she was Lululemon's (LULU) founding lead designer,

The pair has no prenuptial agreement, and how the family’s assets will be divided between the two is not yet finalized, a person familiar with the matter said.

Chip Wilson, who founded Lululemon (LULU) in 1998, resigned from the Vancouver-based firm’s board in 2015 to help his wife and son expand their new business venture, Kit and Ace, a luxury clothing company.

With a stake worth nearly $1B, Chip Wilson owns roughly 9% of Lululemon (LULU) shares, including approximately a 1% stake owned by Summer Wilson valued at nearly $100M.

Shares of the athleisure brand have dropped lately. Lululemon (LULU) lost nearly 17% this week after the company slashed its full-year outlook with Q2 2026 results.

data.title: U.S. hits three Iranian oil tankers after missiles target American warships
data.description:
The U.S. Central Command (Centcom) said that its forces struck three Iranian oil tankers on Saturday after Iran launched ballistic missiles towards two of its Navy warships, signaling the latest retaliatory strikes between the parties this week.

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps has attacked U.S. forces using ballistic missiles throughout the war. However, its attempted attack on the warships is considered a significant escalation in the month-long conflict, U.S. officials said, according to The Wall Street Journal.

The strikes — a day after U.S. President Donald Trump sought to minimize the conflict as “small potatoes” — keep up a new tilt back toward fighting after six months of on-again, off-again war that began with U.S. and Israeli attacks on the country on Feb. 28. Both sides have sought to inflict both military and economic pain, and negotiations have collapsed.

The military’s statement said that an American aircraft carrier and a destroyer evaded “multiple unprovoked Iranian attacks” while patrolling in the region and no U.S. personnel were hurt. It said that two Iranian oil carriers were “permanently disabled” and the third, unladen one, was destroyed.

The U.S. statement said that the tankers were part of a shadow network helping to fund Iran’s powerful Revolutionary Guard and its armed proxies in the region.

There was no immediate Iranian response.

Iran had reported a strike near Kharg Island:

Earlier, Iranian state television had said that four U.S. missiles struck a tanker about 6 miles (10 kilometers) from Kharg Island, home to a terminal through which the country exports most of its oil. Kharg Island has been repeatedly targeted during the war, including U.S. strikes on military sites there in March.

The U.S. said that one tanker was struck off Kharg Island and another was struck near Jask, east of the Strait of Hormuz. The unladen tanker was hit in the Gulf of Oman, and the U.S. said its crew had been “directed to abandon ship.” The statement shared what it called video footage of the strikes.

After the U.S. statement, Iran’s state broadcaster reported the two other tankers attacked, saying their crews had evacuated.

“We will not hesitate to defend American forces, and if necessary, destroy Iran’s limited and exposed oil fleet,” said Adm. Brad Cooper, the head of U.S. Central Command.

The strikes came nearly a week after the U.S. and Iran resumed attacks following a month of relative calm, with the Strait of Hormuz and Iranian communities along it again being targeted. At least five people were killed earlier in the week during a U.S. bombardment of southern Iran. One strike hit a wedding.

Masoumeh Zarei, 13, was wounded in the attack. She spoke to The Associated Press at a hospital while being treated for injuries to her abdomen.

She said that the wedding celebration had already begun when she set out to join it. She never made it there. She was knocked unconscious when a telecommunications tower was struck. Her next memory was of waking up in a hospital.

“The party had just started, and we wanted to go there,” Zarei said, her voice hoarse. “I had made my nails really pretty for the party, but everything changed.”

Her friend, 14-year-old Kiana Karimi, also was wounded and in intensive care. She told the AP that she heard five explosions.

“The first three explosions at the telecommunications tower threw us to the ground,” Karimi said. “I quickly got up to pick my brothers up off the ground. Then there were two more explosions, and after that I don’t remember anything.”

U.S. had tried to turn to economic pressure

The resumption of fighting in the past week came after new U.S. efforts to apply economic pressures on Tehran, whose hard-line new senior leaders have signaled the willingness to dig in after weathering decades of sanctions. The elected government of Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, however, has said that it favors a negotiated end to the war.

Iran has found ways over the years to circumvent sanctions — and now a U.S. blockade of its ports — and get its oil to buyers to help ease growing economic pressures. That relies in part on a shadow fleet transporting its oil.

Meanwhile, the issue that helped lead to the war — Iran's nuclear program — was meant to be addressed in negotiations that fell apart soon after the U.S. and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding in mid-June. Now diplomats say the U.S., Britain, France and Germany seek to refer Iran to the U.N. Security Council for failure to comply with its nuclear nonproliferation obligations.

Instead, Tehran's new leverage focuses on the strait that is crucial to global oil and natural gas shipments and was seen as an international waterway before the war began.

The U.S. military has been helping to guide ships through the strait as Tehran asserts control and targets some vessels, but overall traffic remains low.

The Associated Press contributed to this story.

data.title: Energy sector outperforms in August as Middle East tensions boost oil prices
data.description:
The energy sector (XLE) advanced about 9% in the month of August, compared to a 1% rise in the broader market (SP500), finishing as the top-performing market sector.

The move was driven largely by heightened geopolitical tensions and concerns over oil supply disruptions. Crude oil (CL1:COM) rose towards $90 a barrel, bringing its monthly gain to over 2%, following renewed U.S. military strikes against targets in Iran after provocations in the Strait of Hormuz.

Energy Sector Scorecard

  • Sector Return: +8.8%

  • Best Performer: APA (+24.85%)

  • Worst Performer: Texas Pacific Land (-7.13%)

  • Top Theme: Geopolitical uncertainty

"The energy sector rose 8.8% in August amidst renewed tensions in the Strait of Hormuz. Throughout the month, vessel traffic remained more than 10% below pre-war levels. Furthermore, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait—a key alternative route—is grappling with even greater tensions caused by the Houthis," explained Seeking Alpha analyst Multiplo Invest.

Top energy performers of the month

On the individual front, APA (APA) was the biggest winner in August, gaining nearly 21%. It was followed by Phillips 66 (PSX), which gained 18.5% in the last month.

"APA posted the sector's best performance for the month, climbing 24.85%. The rise in crude oil prices was amplified in the company's results due to its operating leverage, not to mention its valuation multiples, which are discounted relative to peers."

"Meanwhile, Phillips 66 rose 24.36%—the second-highest gain of the month—driven by a different dynamic. Tensions in the Strait of Hormuz act as a significant headwind for refined product output; consequently, the company benefited for another month from expanding refining margins," the analyst added.

Here are the top gainers of the month:

  • APA (APA): +24.85% - Quant rating: Strong Buy with a score of 3.31 out of 5

  • Phillips 66 (PSX): +24.38% - Quant rating: Strong Buy with a score of 4.95 out of 5

  • Marathon Petroleum (MPC): +23.80% - Quant rating: Strong Buy with a score of 4.98 out of 5

  • Valero Energy (VLO): +18.58% - Quant rating: Strong Buy with a score of 4.97 out of 5

  • ConocoPhillips (COP): +16.33% - Quant rating: Buy with a score of 4.47 out of 5

Top energy detractor of the month

On the other hand, Texas Pacific Land (TPL) was the only detractor in August, slipping 7% in the month.

"Texas Pacific Land was the sector's biggest laggard, falling 7.13%. It is important to distinguish its business model: the company owns land and earns royalties on its lessees' production. Therefore, it does not benefit directly from rising oil prices—its lessees do," Multiplo Invest noted.

  • Texas Pacific Land (TPL): -7.13% - Quant rating: Sell with a score of 2.26 out of 5

Looking ahead

Energy stocks are likely to remain sensitive to geopolitical developments, crude oil prices and OPEC+ policy in September. Continued disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz could support oil prices and energy equities, while any de-escalation could pressure the sector after its strong August gains.
